---
title: "Quiz: conditioning, guidance and latent diffusion"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** How can a single network provide both the conditional and the unconditional prediction needed for classifier-free guidance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the label during training?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
During training the label is replaced by "none" at random (say 10 % of the time). The network then learns to denoise both with and without the label; at sampling time it is evaluated twice per step.
:::

---

**Q2.** Compute the guided noise prediction for $\hat\varepsilon_\text{cond} = 0.3$, $\hat\varepsilon_\text{uncond} = 0.1$, $w = 2$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$(1+w)\hat\varepsilon_\text{cond} - w\hat\varepsilon_\text{uncond}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$3 \cdot 0.3 - 2 \cdot 0.1 = 0.7$.
:::

---

**Q3.** Guidance makes samples "more typical" of the class. Typical in which sense?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Most frequent, or most clearly recognisable?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Most clearly recognisable: guidance favours points where the classifier is most certain of the label, i.e. far from the other classes. That is not the most frequent member; with large $w$ it lies beyond the class mean, more extreme than real members.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does recall of a class drop with guidance, while precision may stay high?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which real members are borderline?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Real members that resemble other classes (borderline) are where the label is uncertain; guidance moves samples away from them, so they are no longer covered (recall drops). The remaining samples still lie on real class members (precision stays high) until $w$ is so large that they leave the data.
:::

---

**Q5.** Name two reasons why image generators run diffusion in a latent space.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Cost, and what the diffusion model spends its capacity on.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Far fewer numbers per step (e.g. 48 times), so each step is cheaper; and the diffusion model models layout and content while the autoencoder handles imperceptible pixel detail.
:::

---

**Q6.** In a latent diffusion model, where does the finest detail of a generated image come from?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can the latent represent?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From the decoder: whatever the latent cannot represent is filled in by the decoder's habits, learned from its training images.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why do latent diffusion samples land on realistic codes, whereas decoding draws from the VAE's $\mathcal N(0, I)$ prior can give nonsense?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which distribution does each sample from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The diffusion model learns the actual cloud of training codes (the aggregate posterior). The VAE prior is a round Gaussian that also covers regions with no codes; decoding such points gives shapes no training image had.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* What density does classifier-free guidance target, written with the classifier $p(y\mid\mathbf x)$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Bayes in $p(\mathbf x\mid y)^{1+w}p(\mathbf x)^{-w}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$p(\mathbf x\mid y)\,p(y\mid\mathbf x)^w$ (up to normalisation): the class density sharpened by the classifier's confidence. Applying the combination at every noise level does not sample it exactly.
:::
